steps: Mercury, bromine and gallium are elements that can exist as liquids near ordinary room temperature.
Mercury and bromine are liquid at ordinary room temperature; gallium melts just above it.
Transition elements have partially filled d-orbitals in their atoms or in at least one of their ions.
They differ from normal elements because they commonly show variable oxidation states and form coloured compounds.
Many transition elements and their compounds also act as catalysts.
items.finalAnswer: Transition elements have partially filled d-orbitals and commonly show variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic properties.

steps: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.
Chlorine gains electrons more readily and can displace bromine from a bromide salt.
For example: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.
items.finalAnswer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.

steps: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen; iodine is the least reactive among the commonly studied halogens.
Down the group, atomic size increases and the attraction of the nucleus for an incoming electron decreases.
Therefore, the tendency of halogen atoms to gain an electron and form halide ions decreases down the group.
items.finalAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive and iodine is the least reactive among the commonly studied halogens.

steps: A catalytic converter is fitted in the exhaust system of an automobile.
It contains catalysts, such as platinum, palladium and rhodium, which convert harmful exhaust gases into less harmful substances.
Carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons are converted into carbon dioxide and water; nitrogen oxides are converted into nitrogen.
items.finalAnswer: A catalytic converter uses catalysts to change harmful automobile exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

steps: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell and react by losing it.
Down the group, atomic size increases and the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily; hence reactivity increases.
Halogens react by gaining one electron to complete their outermost shell.
Down the group, atomic size increases and the attraction for an incoming electron decreases; hence the tendency to gain an electron, and their reactivity, decreases.
items.finalAnswer: Alkali-metal reactivity increases down the group because their outer electron is lost more easily, whereas halogen reactivity decreases because attraction for an incoming electron becomes weaker.

steps: Metals generally have strong metallic bonds: positive metal ions are held together by attraction to a sea of delocalised electrons.
These strong forces make metals generally tough and strong.
Non-metals generally lack metallic bonding; many consist of atoms or molecules held together by comparatively weaker forces.
Therefore, solid non-metals are generally brittle and are neither tough nor strong.
items.finalAnswer: Strong metallic bonding makes metals generally tough and strong, while non-metals generally lack this bonding and are brittle.

steps: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell and readily lose it to form positive ions.
By donating electrons, alkali metals act as reducing agents.
Halogens need one electron to complete their outermost shell and readily gain it to form negative ions.
By accepting electrons, halogens act as oxidising agents.
Thus, alkali metals and halogens react in opposite ways and combine to form ionic compounds.
items.finalAnswer: Alkali metals donate electrons and act as reducing agents, whereas halogens accept electrons and act as oxidising agents.
